jobs.brief: Six pillars with numbered icons (ID band, speech bubble, red-label vial, surgical checklist, hands, yellow band) — no NotebookLM frames reused
jobs.alt_text: Six patient safety goals as six pillars.
jobs.prompt:
Create six separate simple pictogram illustrations arranged as a balanced set of six vertical pillars, with no labels or numerals: (1) patient identification wristband, (2) speech bubble for effective communication, (3) medicine vial with a small safety check, (4) surgical checklist, (5) hands supporting a patient, (6) a clinic quality-improvement cycle represented by a circular arrow. Do not assert that these icons alone define the official patient-safety goals. Leave every label to the editable course layer. Use the shared style suffix with caring purple #652D8C.

Flat vector illustration for a Saudi outpatient healthcare e-learning course, 16:9 landscape, clean minimalist composition, simple geometric shapes, thin navy (#003867) outlines, white and very light blue-grey (#F4F7FA, #C0CED9) surfaces, one approved module highlight colour, lots of white space, calm bright clinic environment, soft even lighting. Generic fictional people only, modest culturally appropriate clothing. No text, letters, numbers, logos, My Clinic wordmark, signage words, watermark, readable interface, patient or staff identifiers. No photorealism, 3D render, gradients, neon, clutter, heavy shadow, blood, injury, distorted hands, extra objects or hazards beyond the brief, or Western hospital stereotypes. Keep the composition readable at 960 × 540; leave negative space for separately typeset screen content. Deliver an unlabelled PNG master and source/settings, and record generator, date and provenance.

voices: Noor — female, early-to-mid 30s, warm, calm, clear
jobs.script: NOOR: Hello, I'm Noor, a senior nurse and patient-safety liaison. Welcome to clinical governance: how My Clinic protects patients every day. You'll link daily decisions to quality, safety, risk and reporting.
jobs.format: MP3 44.1 kHz mono 96 kbps, −16 LUFS integrated, −1 dBTP, 300 ms head/tail
jobs.captions: WebVTT from the final audio (forced alignment), speaker names as <v Noor>/<v Dr. Omar>

voices: Noor — female, early-to-mid 30s, warm, calm, clear
jobs.script: NOOR: Clinical governance connects the way a service is organised with the way care is delivered and the results patients experience. It asks teams to use reliable information, learn from problems and improve practice over time. Keep one question in mind: what helps the next patient receive safe, consistent care? The standard is a daily way of working, not a slogan.
jobs.format: MP3 44.1 kHz mono 96 kbps, −16 LUFS integrated, −1 dBTP, 300 ms head/tail
jobs.captions: WebVTT from the final audio (forced alignment), speaker names as <v Noor>/<v Dr. Omar>

voices: Noor — female, early-to-mid 30s, warm, calm, clear
jobs.script: NOOR: Most of us have stayed quiet about something unsafe at least once. I have. Speaking up gets easier every time. Answer honestly, or pass.
jobs.format: MP3 44.1 kHz mono 96 kbps, −16 LUFS integrated, −1 dBTP, 300 ms head/tail
jobs.captions: WebVTT from the final audio (forced alignment), speaker names as <v Noor>/<v Dr. Omar>

voices: Noor — female, early-to-mid 30s, warm, calm, clear
jobs.script: NOOR: Start with structure: the resources and setting available to provide care. Processes describe what the team does and how consistently it is done. Outcomes describe the results for patients. The three layers connect, but they answer different questions. Reliable, valid data helps a team understand actual performance rather than rely on impressions. The improvement cycle shown here connects measurement to action; confirm its approved step names before production. The arrow shows how measurement supports improvement over time.
jobs.format: MP3 44.1 kHz mono 96 kbps, −16 LUFS integrated, −1 dBTP, 300 ms head/tail
jobs.captions: WebVTT from the final audio (forced alignment), speaker names as <v Noor>/<v Dr. Omar>

voices: Dr. Omar — male, late 30s, friendly, confident, medium-low pitch
jobs.script: OMAR: Let's score one together. It's a made-up case: expired items turn up twice this month in a clinic fridge. Impact first. A patient could get a vaccine that doesn't work, so we call impact four. It has already happened twice, so likelihood is three. Four times three gives twelve. Honestly, the number alone doesn't tell you what to do. The band for twelve comes from our corporate matrix, which Risk is still confirming. Then choose a response that lowers the risk, such as a weekly checklist with a second check. Treat those controls as teaching examples until Quality and Risk approve them.
jobs.format: MP3 44.1 kHz mono 96 kbps, −16 LUFS integrated, −1 dBTP, 300 ms head/tail
